h: Scandal, song and a lazy afternoon on the Thames
p: Cliveden's history is full of headline moments. "Rule, Britannia!" was first performed in the grounds here in 1740, when the estate belonged to Frederick, Prince of Wales. In the 20th century it became the home of the Astors, and Nancy Astor, the first woman to take her seat as an MP, hosted politicians, writers and celebrities here in the 1920s and 1930s. Then, in 1961, a meeting by the swimming pool set off the Profumo affair, one of the biggest political scandals of the century.

The mansion itself is now a luxury hotel run separately, so the National Trust visit is mostly about the gardens and woodland. Don't let that put you off, because the grounds are huge and there's loads to see. Look out for the Fountain of Love, a grand marble and shell sculpture, the Long Garden with its topiary, and the Water Garden with its pagoda.

Allow at least half a day. The paths can be steep in places as they drop down towards the river, so wear sensible shoes and leave a bit of energy for the climb back up. It's a lovely spot for a picnic, and the views across the Thames valley are worth bringing a camera for.

Nearby, Maidenhead has plenty of places to eat, and the riverside around Boulter's Lock is great for a gentle stroll watching boats come and go. The Thames Path runs along this stretch too, so walkers can easily stretch the day out. Cookham, the pretty riverside village loved by the painter Stanley Spencer, is just up the river.
